t: "The Elder": a title, not a name
p: The writer gives no name, only a title. He expects the readers to know at once who "the Elder" is.
b: Ho presbyteros means "the older man" and was also the word for a church leader, an "elder" (Acts 14:23; 1 Timothy 5:17). With the article it is a title: not "an elder" among many, but the one everyone knew. Readers take it three ways. (1) Age and standing: one of the first generation, who had seen and heard Jesus, as the opening of 1 John claims (Armin Baum, in The Oxford Handbook of Hebrews and the Catholic Epistles, 2024). (2) An office: Westcott, as Plummer quotes him, thought it "describes not age simply but official position." (3) A different man: Papias spoke of "the presbyter John" as well as the apostle John, and Eusebius and Jerome took him for a second John at Ephesus, to whom some in Jerome's day gave these two letters. The same title opens 3 John, so one man wrote both. The book page sets out the authorship question.

p: "To an elect lady": the Greek has no article. Readers since about 200 have asked who she is.
b: Eklektē kyria can be read four ways. (1) A church, pictured as a woman, with its members as "her children" and a sister church sending greetings (1:13); the church is a mother in Galatians 4:26 ("She is our mother"). (2) A real Christian woman and her family, as Ellicott's commentary and the Expositor's Bible read it. (3) A woman named Kyria ("Lady"): a work handed down under Athanasius' name says John "writes to Kyria," Bengel says the Syriac version kept the word as a name, and Young's Literal Translation prints it as one. (4) A woman named Electa ("Chosen"): Clement of Alexandria, in comments that survive only in Latin, wrote that the letter went "to a Babylonian lady, by name Electa." Plummer answered that her sister (1:13) is also "chosen," and two sisters both named Electa is hard to believe. The Plain keeps "the chosen lady" so every reading stays open.

p: "Truth" comes five times in thirteen verses. Here, with no article, it means "truly, with a love that is real."
b: Alētheia, "truth," is the word 2 John is built on: twice in this verse, then in 1:2, 1:3 and 1:4. Without the article (en alētheia) it describes the love: real and sincere, the way 1 John 3:18 joins love with "truth." With the article it is "the truth," the faith revealed in Jesus, which believers come to know: "You will come to know the truth" (John 8:32). The Plain keeps the difference: "in truth" where the Greek has no article, "the truth" where it has one. 3 John opens with the same words to Gaius (3 John 1:1), and Jesus calls himself "the truth" (John 14:6).

a: the truth that remains in us
p: Menō, "remain," is the Gospel of John's word for staying joined to Jesus. Here the truth itself is what stays.
b: The verb menō, "remain, stay, live on," is one of John's favorite words: "Remain in me, and I in you" (John 15:4). In this letter the truth "remains in us" (1:2), and the test of a teacher is whether he "remains in the teaching" (1:9). The Plain uses "remain" every time, as the Gospel of John does, so a reader can follow the word through. The KJV's "dwelleth" (here) and "abideth" (1:9) render the same Greek.
orig: τὴν μένουσαν ἐν ἡμῖν (tēn menousan en hēmin)

a: will be with us for all time
t: An echo of the Advocate promise
p: Jesus promised the Advocate would be with the disciples "for all time." The Elder says the same of the truth.
b: The Greek meth' hēmōn estai eis ton aiōna is close to Jesus' promise in John 14:16: "he will give you another Advocate to be with you for all time." The next verse names him: "He is the Spirit of truth" (John 14:17). Plummer heard the echo, and so took "the truth" here as the truth revealed in Christ and kept alive in believers by the Spirit. The Plain uses the Gospel's wording, "for all time," so the link shows.

p: Most letters say "Grace to you." The Elder says these gifts "will be" with us, and counts himself in.
b: Paul's letters open with a wish, "Grace to you and peace." Here the verb is a future, "will be": a confident promise, and "us" includes the writer. The three gifts come in the same order only in the letters to Timothy: "Grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord" (1 Timothy 1:2; 2 Timothy 1:2). Jude has mercy, peace and love (Jude 1:2). Plummer explains them as God's favor to sinners, his pity for their misery, and the peace that follows. "Grace" is rare in John's writings. Ordinary Greek letters opened with one word, chairein, "greetings" (see 1:10).
orig: ἔσται μεθ' ἡμῶν χάρις ἔλεος εἰρήνη (estai meth' hēmōn charis eleos eirēnē)

p: This exact phrase appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It may already answer the deceivers of 1:7.
b: The Greek tou huiou tou patros occurs only here in the New Testament (a search of the SBL Greek text finds no other place). The writer also repeats "from" (para): grace comes "from God the Father and from Jesus Christ," two persons named side by side. Plummer suggests the fullness is deliberate, because the letter is about to warn against those who deny Jesus Christ coming in the flesh (1:7) and so do not have "both the Father and the Son" (1:9; compare 1 John 2:22-23).
orig: τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ πατρός (tou huiou tou patros)

p: The verb for the Elder's joy here is the same one he forbids the lady to say to a deceiver in 1:10.
b: Echarēn, "I was glad," is from chairō, "rejoice." Its infinitive chairein, "rejoice!", was the everyday greeting that opened a Greek letter (Acts 15:23, "greetings"). In 1:10-11 the Elder says not to say chairein to a false teacher. English cannot keep the play, but a Greek hearer would notice that the word for the joy the Elder feels over faithful children is the word he will not let her give to deceivers. 3 John 1:3 opens with the same words, "I was very glad."

p: The Greek says "of your children," meaning some of them. Was the rest of the family going astray?
b: Ek tōn teknōn sou means "some of your children," not all. Plummer weighed both readings. It may be a gentle hint that only some were walking in truth, which would fit the warnings that follow (1:7-11). Or the Elder may simply have met only some of them, perhaps where he lived, as the children of the lady's sister are with him (1:13). If the lady is a church, the "children" are its members, and the hint is of a congregation already divided.
orig: ἐκ τῶν τέκνων σου (ek tōn teknōn sou)

t: "Walking": a Jewish way to speak of life
p: To "walk" is to live, an old Hebrew idiom. Jewish law is still called halakhah, "the walking."
b: The image comes from the Hebrew Bible, where halakh, "walk," is the common word for how a person lives: Enoch "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24), and Israel is to keep to "the road the LORD your God commanded you to walk in" (Deuteronomy 13:5). The rabbis' word for the rules of daily life, halakhah, comes from the same verb. Jesus' followers kept the idiom. 2 John uses "walk" three times (1:4, and twice in 1:6) and 3 John twice (3 John 1:3-4). The Plain keeps the image instead of turning it into "living."

t: A command received from the Father
p: Jesus spoke of the command he "received from my Father." Now believers have received one too.
b: In John's Gospel Jesus says of his life, "This is the command I received from my Father" (John 10:18), and of his words, "The Father who sent me, he himself, gave me a command" (John 12:49). The Elder uses the same language for the church: "we received a command from the Father." The next two verses say what it is: to love each other (1:5), and to walk in it (1:6). "Command" (entolē) appears four times in these three verses. The Plain uses "command," as the Gospel of John does (John 13:34).

p: The Elder addresses her directly. The letter shifts between "you" singular and "you" plural.
b: Kyria here is a direct address, the feminine of kyrios, "lord, sir." Greek, unlike modern English, shows whether "you" is one person or many. 2 John speaks to "you" singular in 1:4-5 and 1:13, and to "you" plural in 1:6, 1:8, 1:10 and 1:12. Readers who take the lady as a church say the plural shows she stands for a group. Plummer, who left the question open, thought the change fits a mother and her family just as well.

p: Jesus called "love each other" a new command. The Elder calls it one they had from the beginning.
b: Jesus told his disciples, "I am giving you a new command: that you love each other" (John 13:34). For the Elder's readers it is no longer new: it is the command "we have had from the beginning," since the day they first heard the good news. 1 John 2:7-8 makes the same point at greater length: the command is old, and it is also new. "From the beginning" in these letters usually means the beginning of the readers' life as believers (1 John 2:24; 1 John 3:11), though 1 John 1:1 reaches back to the beginning itself.
r: John 13:34; John 15:12; John 15:17; 1 John 2:7-8; 1 John 3:11; 1 John 3:23

t: Love that obeys, obedience that loves
p: 1:5 says the command is to love; 1:6 says love is keeping the commands. The circle is deliberate.
b: In 1:5 the command is love. In 1:6 love is walking by the commands. Plummer called this "no vicious logical circle, but a healthy moral connexion." It is the same circle Jesus draws in John's Gospel: "If you love me, you will keep the commands I give" (John 14:15), and "The person who has my commands and keeps them, that is someone who loves me" (John 14:21). 1 John 5:3 says it again. For the Elder, love is not first a feeling; it is a way of walking.

p: "It" could be love or the command. Both Greek nouns are feminine, so grammar cannot decide.
b: En autē, "in it," points back to a feminine noun, and two are near: "love" (agapē) and "the command" (entolē). Plummer argued for love: John speaks of walking "in" truth, light or darkness, but "by" (kata) the commands, never "in" them, and the verse began with love. Others read "the command," the nearest noun. Since the command is to love, the sense comes out the same either way. The Plain keeps "it," as the Greek does.
orig: ἵνα ἐν αὐτῇ περιπατῆτε (hina en autē peripatēte)

t: Deceivers, or men who lead astray
p: Planos means one who leads others astray. The chief priests used it of Jesus himself.
b: Planos comes from the verb "to lead astray, make wander," and can also mean an impostor. It is rare in the New Testament: the chief priests call Jesus "that deceiver" (Matthew 27:63), and Paul says he and his coworkers are treated as deceivers (2 Corinthians 6:8). Jesus had warned that false messiahs and false prophets would come "to lead the chosen astray, if that were possible" (Mark 13:22). 1 John uses the related verb for those who lead believers astray (1 John 2:26; 1 John 3:7). The Elder names their mark in the next words: they do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh.

p: 1 John 4:2 says Jesus Christ "has come" in the flesh; here the Greek is a present participle, "coming."
b: 1 John 4:2 uses a perfect participle (elēlythota, "having come"); 2 John 7 uses a present one (erchomenon, "coming"). Readers explain the change three ways. (1) The present is timeless: the deceivers deny the person, Jesus Christ as the one who comes in the flesh, and not only a past event. Plummer pressed this point, and noted that Christ is said to come "in" the flesh, never "into" it. (2) It points to the second coming: Oecumenius took the participle as a future, of Christ's return (Meyer's commentary reports this and calls it incorrect). (3) There is no real difference; John uses the two forms for the same confession. The KJV's "is come" smooths it into the perfect. Polycarp, early in the 100s, wrote, "whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist" (Philippians 7.1), close to both verses.
orig: Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐρχόμενον ἐν σαρκί (Iēsoun Christon erchomenon en sarki)

p: Only John's letters use the word. Here it names anyone who denies Christ coming in the flesh, not one figure at the end.
b: Antichristos occurs only in 1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3 and here. 1 John says "many antichrists" have already come. Here the singular follows a plural: "many deceivers... This one is the deceiver and the antichrist." Plummer saw two possible senses: each such teacher is the deceiver and the antichrist, or all of them together are. Later Christians joined the word to Daniel's "little horn" and Paul's "man of lawlessness" (Daniel 7:8; 2 Thessalonians 2:3) and looked for one great enemy at the end; the topic page traces that history. In this verse the word describes teachers already at work, and the site prints it in lower case.

a: Be on your guard for yourselves
p: The Greek is nearly word for word Jesus' own warning about the end.
b: Blepete heautous is what Jesus says in Mark 13:9, where Mark adds "But you" (de hymeis): "But you, be on your guard for yourselves," in the speech where he warns that false messiahs will lead people astray (Mark 13:22). Plummer noted the match. The Plain uses Mark's wording so a reader can hear it. The danger here is not persecution but deception from within.

p: Misthos is a worker's pay. The Elder pictures the work done and the pay to come.
b: Misthos is pay for work (Luke 10:7: "a worker has earned his pay"). In the text the Plain follows, "we" did the work and "you" receive the pay: the first teachers labored, and the readers will be paid in full if they hold on. Plummer took the full reward to be eternal life, set beside the real but partial rewards of this life (Mark 10:29-30). Others read it of the reward for faithful service given at the judgment (Matthew 10:41; 1 Corinthians 3:8). See the variant: copyists changed the persons of the verbs so the sentence would run smoothly.

t: Christ's teaching, or teaching about Christ?
p: Greek "of" can mean either. Is it what Christ taught, or the confession about him in 1:7?
b: Hē didachē tou Christou can mean the teaching Christ gave (Plummer's choice, comparing John 18:19 and Revelation 2:14-15) or the teaching about Christ: that he comes in the flesh (1:7). Many readers prefer the second because of the context. Irenaeus says Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia, divided Jesus, a man born of Joseph and Mary, from "Christ," who "descended upon him in the form of a dove" and left him before he suffered (Against Heresies 1.26.1): the kind of teaching the Elder may have in mind. Either way, the test is the same: whether a teacher "remains" in what the readers had from the beginning (1:5-6).
orig: ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ Χριστοῦ (en tē didachē tou Christou)

p: To "have" God is John's way of speaking of a living bond, not ownership.
b: John's letters speak of "having" the Father and the Son: 1 John 2:23 says that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, and 1 John 5:12 that whoever has the Son has life. Plummer warned against weakening the phrase to "does not know God": it means not having God as one's God at all. The second half of the verse turns it around: whoever remains in the teaching has "both the Father and the Son," the pair already named side by side in 1:3.

a: do not take him into the house
p: No "your" in the Greek: "into a house." The house was likely where the church met, and teachers came to stay.
b: Christians met in homes for their first two centuries, and traveling teachers depended on hosts for a bed and food (3 John 1:5-8). To take a teacher into the house meant giving him a base and a hearing, and the church would assume he came with the host's approval. The Didache, an early Christian manual, has similar rules: whoever teaches what has been handed down is to be received, "But if the teacher himself turn and teach another doctrine to the destruction of this, hear him not" (11.1-2); everyone who comes in the Lord's name is to be received and then tested (12.1). Plummer thought "comes" here means coming as a teacher on a mission, not a passing visit.

p: Chairein was the word that opened a Greek letter, "Greetings!" Saying it meant a welcome.
b: Chairein (literally "rejoice!") opens the letter of the Jerusalem council: "to the brothers of Gentile birth in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings" (Acts 15:23). To say it to someone was to wish him well and treat him as a friend. Plummer thought the rule covers any act that would seem to approve the false teaching, not a refusal of common courtesy. Clement of Alexandria's comment on this verse advises against discussing divine things with such people, or praying with them. See the chapter page for how the rule has been applied, and 1:4 for the play on "I was very glad."
orig: χαίρειν αὐτῷ μὴ λέγετε (chairein autō mē legete)

p: Koinōneō is the verb of koinōnia, "fellowship." To welcome the deceiver is to join his work.
b: Koinōnei comes from the word for fellowship (koinōnia, 1 John 1:3). "Evil" (ponēros) is the word used for "the evil one" in 1 John 2:13-14. Early Christians quoted this verse as an apostle's rule. Irenaeus (about 180) gives it as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple: "He that bids them be of good-speed is a partaker with their evil deeds" (Against Heresies 1.16.3). At the council of Carthage in 256, Bishop Aurelius of Chullabi quoted 1:10 to argue that people who must not be taken into a house cannot be admitted into God's house without the church's baptism. Stephen, bishop of Rome, held the opposite practice (see the chapter page).
orig: κοινωνεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ τοῖς πονηροῖς (koinōnei tois ergois autou tois ponērois)

p: Chartēs, "paper," was a sheet of papyrus. This is the only time the word appears in the New Testament.
b: Chartēs was papyrus, the Egyptian writing material made from strips of reed pressed together. Plummer notes that the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, though the Greek Old Testament uses it in Jeremiah 36:23; parchment, the costlier material, is named in 2 Timothy 4:13 ("especially the parchments"). Ink (melan, "black") was made with soot. 2 and 3 John are almost the same length, and A. E. Brooke suggested that this is because each was written to fit on one sheet of papyrus. A letter of recommendation from Egypt of about AD 25, Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292, is written on a sheet about 20 by 15 centimeters.
orig: διὰ χάρτου καὶ μέλανος (dia chartou kai melanos)

p: The Greek says "mouth to mouth," a Hebrew idiom for speaking in person, used of God and Moses.
b: Stoma pros stoma is literally "mouth to mouth." It is not the "face to face" of 1 Corinthians 13:12. It is a Hebrew idiom. Of Moses God says, "Mouth to mouth I speak with him, / openly and not in riddles" (Numbers 12:8), where the Greek Old Testament has stoma kata stoma. The exact Greek words of this verse, stoma pros stoma, are in the Greek of Jeremiah 32:4 (39:4 in the Greek numbering): Zedekiah "will speak with him mouth to mouth," with the king of Babylon. Here it simply means in person. The same words end 3 John (3 John 1:14). The Plain uses the English idiom "face to face" in both letters.

p: The Greek matches Jesus' words in John 16:24, "so that your joy will be filled up."
b: Hina hē chara... peplērōmenē ē is the wording of John 16:24: "Keep asking and you will receive, so that your joy will be filled up" (compare John 15:11; John 17:13). 1 John 1:4 gives the same purpose for that letter. Whether the Elder wrote "our joy" or "your joy" is a variant: see the entry on "our joy." Either way, a letter is second best; full joy comes from being together.

p: If the lady is a church, her sister is a church too: the one where the Elder is writing.
b: On the reading that the "chosen lady" is a church, her "chosen sister" is the Elder's own congregation, which sends greetings through its members, "the children." Readers note that the sister herself sends no greeting, which suits a church better than a woman. Plummer answered that the sister might be away or dead, while her children lived where the Elder was. 1 Peter 5:13 sends greetings from a woman "chosen" with the readers "in Babylon," which many take to be a church as well. One manuscript (minuscule 307) and some Vulgate copies read "the church" here, and a note in the margin of minuscule 465 adds "in Ephesus" (see the variant).
orig: τῆς ἀδελφῆς σου τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς (tēs adelphēs sou tēs eklektēs)
